a3258.speaker: Unicef (UN children's agency)
a3258.speech: Has called for "urgent action" in the country to "protect the health and future of every child in Botswana"; it noted that "malnutrition is a daily struggle" in the town of D'Kar, saying "the president's call underscores what we witness on the ground".

a3346.speaker: Doulaye Sanou, president of the SAMAO 2025 organising committee
a3346.speech: Said this edition will constitute a framework for exchanging experiences between public and private actors from various countries for the sustainable management of mineral resources. ; "It will serve as a platform for mining industry actors to discuss the issue of the rehabilitation and closure of mines, with the future of local communities as the backdrop." ; Indicated that at least 2,000 participants from Burkina Faso, the sub-region and the rest of the world are expected at SAMAO, at the Ouaga 2000 International Conference Centre; added that a session will be devoted to presenting innovations for more environmentally friendly mining, and that the countries of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) will be honoured through a session dedicated to their achievements in mine rehabilitation.

a3346.speaker: Doulaye Sanou, president of the SAMAO 2025 organising committee
a3346.speech: Explained that the pre-SAMAO workshop aims to contribute to the development of local materials in Burkina Faso's cement industry. ; "It will thus make it possible, among other things, to make known the existing potential of quarry substances that can be used in cement manufacturing and to explore the economic and industrial opportunities linked to the exploitation of local resources in order to reduce dependence on imports and strengthen the capacity of national industries."

a3551.speaker: Qatar and the United States (mediating countries)
a3551.speech: Provided the details under which the ceasefire is to proceed in three phases.

a3551.speaker: Two sources close to Hamas (anonymous), cited by AFP
a3551.speech: Said the first group of hostages released should be made up of three Israeli women, but that the time of their release is not yet known.

a3551.speaker: Israeli Justice Ministry
a3551.speech: Specified that the release of the first Palestinian prisoners would not take place before 3 p.m. (French time).

a3551.speaker: Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Prime Minister of Qatar
a3551.speech: Explained that the first phase includes the opening of negotiations on the terms of the second phase, namely “a definitive end to the war” ; “the details concerning phases two and three will be finalised during the implementation of the first phase.”

a3551.speaker: Several mediating countries
a3551.speech: Agreed on Friday to set up a joint operations room in Cairo, Egypt, to “ensure effective coordination” and compliance with the terms of the truce.

a3551.speaker: Joe Biden, US President
a3551.speech: “Over the next six weeks, Israel will negotiate the necessary arrangements to move to phase two, which will mark the definitive end of the war. I repeat, a definitive end to the war.” ; “When phase two begins, there will be an exchange for the release of the remaining hostages still alive, including male soldiers, and all remaining Israeli forces will withdraw from Gaza. The temporary ceasefire will then become permanent.”

a3551.speaker: Israeli army (estimates)
a3551.speech: Estimates that 94 people are still held in the enclave since 7 October, and Israel has already declared 34 hostages dead.

a3586.speaker: Carl Anderson, USAID resident representative
a3586.speech: "Community health programmes are indispensable for making progress towards universal health coverage and achieving the SDGs."

a3586.speaker: Benjamin Hounkpatin, Minister of Health of Benin
a3586.speech: rejoices that the National Community Health Policy will help change the Beninese approach "to the provision of care and health services to the population, while placing the emphasis on prevention and health promotion and on the establishment of an alert system for the occurrence of diseases in the community setting. It is the expression of a true health revolution which will certainly have an impact on universal health coverage, and at lower cost." ; observes: "The Pnsc commits communal elected officials and local actors to implementing the population's access to preventive, promotional and curative care, to health watch and to the epidemiological surveillance of disease cases."

a3586.speaker: Benjamin Hounkpatin, Minister of Health of Benin
a3586.speech: indicates: "The success of the rollout of this new community health policy depends on the ownership and active involvement of local authorities at every stage of its implementation." ; "Our teams and we ourselves must be constantly engaged at all stages of the rollout of the National Community Health Policy in our departments and communes, particularly during the phase of identifying community relays, counting households, and monitoring the activities of community relays and of qualified community health workers in our villages and boroughs."

a3586.speaker: Veronique Tognifode, Minister of Social Affairs and Microfinance of Benin
a3586.speech: "Making community relays operational is a lever on which the Ministry of Social Affairs will be able to act in order to facilitate the success of the productive social safety net programme, 'Gbesoke'; the project for the employability of persons with disabilities; the Insurance for the Strengthening of Human Capital (Arch) in its health insurance component; and the Alafia Micro-credit."

a3586.speaker: Djanabou Mahonde, UNICEF resident representative
a3586.speech: "These proceedings are crucial for UNICEF and for all the partners, and show the strong commitment and leadership of the government of Benin in strengthening the community health system and primary health care."

a3586.speaker: Raphael Akotegnon, Minister of Decentralisation and Local Governance of Benin
a3586.speech: promises: "As the lead for the monitoring of community health at the level of the departments and communes, I personally undertake to give my best for the coordination of all the actions of my sector falling within this framework."

a3760.speaker: Documents leaked by Congress and analysed by The Independent (UK)
a3760.speech: According to the documents, the U.S. government slashed USAID-backed projects worth more than $400m in famine-affected Somalia this year.

a3760.speaker: South African government (Pretoria)
a3760.speech: Has been putting pressure on Taiwan to move its office out of the capital to Johannesburg, arguing that having it in the administrative seat of government violates the country's one-China principle, adopted in 1998.

a3760.speaker: South African government (Pretoria)
a3760.speech: Insists its relationship with Taiwan is "non-political" and any decision made is based on "fundamentally shifting" economic diplomacy.

a4156.speaker: François Noudégbessi, Minister in charge of Urban Planning and Land Reform of Benin
a4156.speech: Expressed complete satisfaction, even if he fears that possible difficulties may disrupt the installations; insisted several times on the supply of electricity, despite the generator available on site, and on maintaining high-speed telephone communication, hammering home that “these stations must not suffer any failure.”

a4156.speaker: Dah Dossoumon Apollinaire, Director General of the IGN (National Geographic Institute), member of the delegation
a4156.speech: Said: “The permanent station is very important because it will from now on facilitate land management. We therefore urge you to help us preserve it carefully.”

a4156.speaker: Sanni Gounou, Mayor of Kandi
a4156.speech: Believes that these permanent stations will be of great importance for the definitive settlement of land conflicts in his commune and will put an end to the tragedies linked to them.

a4156.speaker: A local elected official (anonymous), Gogounou
a4156.speech: Said that the land plan operations caused some clashes between various landowners, and that cases of death and material damage had been recorded.

a4156.speaker: Members of the MCA-Benin/Ministry delegation
a4156.speech: Deplored these unfortunate facts and expressed their wish to see peace return to the villages concerned ; placed particular emphasis on the need to pursue awareness-raising with much more energy in order to achieve the expected results.

a4156.speaker: Kassoumou Nassirou, representative of the Prefect of Atacora-Donga
a4156.speech: Did not hide his joy: “We thank MCA-Benin and the MCC for all they do for us and all they will also do for us.”

a4156.speaker: Lucien Babagbéto, Ministry of Urban Planning of Benin
a4156.speech: Insisted: “The commissioning of the permanent stations already constitutes a great solution for land tenure security; their maintenance must therefore be a major concern.” ; Later told the press that the question of land insecurity remains a major preoccupation for the government of Dr Boni Yayi.

a4156.speaker: Séyidou Bio Baguiri, Director of the “Access to Land” Project
a4156.speech: Believes that the objective of this tour has been achieved, saying he is happy that the various local authorities met were able to understand the merits of these permanent stations, which will make it possible to draw up rural land plans with a precision never before seen in Benin.

a4224.speaker: USAID (statement posted on the USAID website / directive issued Tuesday night)
a4224.speech: Said that as of 11:59 p.m. ET Friday, “all USAID direct hire personnel will be placed on administrative leave globally, with the exception of designated personnel responsible for mission-critical functions, core leadership and specially designated programs” ; said it is preparing a plan for personnel posted outside the United States “under which the Agency would arrange and pay for return travel to the United States within 30 days” and terminate “contracts that are not determined to be essential” ; the statement ends with: “Thank you for your service.”

a4224.speaker: Congressional Research Service (report)
a4224.speech: Affirmed that it is not legal for the president to unilaterally “abolish, move, or consolidate USAID” and that he needs congressional authorization to do so: “Because Congress established USAID as an independent establishment (defined in 5 U.S.C. 104) within the executive branch, the President does not have the authority to abolish it; congressional authorization would be required to abolish, move, or consolidate USAID.”

a4224.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a4224.speech: Announced on Monday that he would be acting administrator of USAID, confirming the de-facto takeover of the humanitarian agency by the State Department.

a4224.speaker: Peter Marocco, USAID acting deputy administrator (notice/letter to staff)
a4224.speech: “You will remain on administrative leave with pay until otherwise notified,” the notice states ; “During the period that you are on administrative leave you are not to enter USAID premises, access USAID systems, or attempt to use your position or authority with USAID in any way without my prior permission or prior permission of a supervisor in your chain of command” ; the letter instructed employees to email a USAID official with their “personal contact information, including your phone number, email and mailing address,” so they can remain available during regular business hours.

a4224.speaker: CNN (earlier reporting)
a4224.speech: CNN reported earlier that staffers were receiving individual emails Tuesday informing them that they were being put on leave; multiple officials shared with CNN the notice from the acting deputy administrator, Peter Marocco.

a4224.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4224.speech: When a reporter told him on Tuesday that it sounded like he was going to “wind down” the agency, he laughed and said, “Sounds like it.” ; “Look at all the fraud that he’s found in this USAID,” the president said of Elon Musk, adding without evidence, “It has to be corrupt.”

a4224.speaker: One USAID official put on leave (anonymous)
a4224.speech: “People are hysterical. My friends are crying. We don’t know what’s going on”; noted that officials posted abroad may have children in school or spouses with jobs, and now that is “all uprooted” ; “No access to any government system; can’t see emails. It’s like we’re criminals.”

a4224.speaker: A USAID employee (anonymous)
a4224.speech: Told CNN they emailed the USAID official as instructed and got a bounceback, saying that person is also on leave.

a4224.speaker: USAID officials (anonymous)
a4224.speech: Said the sudden chaos has left employees struggling to get any answers.

a4224.speaker: USAID (email sent to staff Tuesday, obtained by CNN)
a4224.speech: Said USAID headquarters and annex offices in the Washington, DC, area will remain closed the remainder of the week — the headquarters in Washington, a second DC annex location, an office in Leesburg, Virginia, and one in Springfield, Virginia: “Agency personnel normally assigned to work at these USAID properties should telework this week” ; noted there are some exceptions for personnel with essential on-site and building maintenance functions and that employees are still “expected to remain available during regular business hours and operations.”

a4224.speaker: Elon Musk, leader of the Department of Governmental Efficiency
a4224.speech: Has led the Trump administration’s effort to weaken USAID, falsely calling it a “viper’s nest of radical-left marxists who hate America” and branding it a “criminal organization” that should “die.”

a4224.speaker: Democrats (US Congress)
a4224.speech: The Trump administration’s actions have raised questions from Democrats over the legality of any wind-down of the agency that will likely have a dramatic consequence for global life-saving aid from the United States.

a4507.speaker: Noël Fonton, Minister responsible for Urban Planning, Housing and Sanitation of Benin
a4507.speech: In his opening remarks, recalled the importance of the various documents to be validated during the session: "Through a strategic plan with deadlines and resources, a formalised decision-making procedure must, from now on and once validated, guide the Institute's various actions up to 2019," the minister stated; for him, results cannot be achieved in an organisation without qualified human resources, and he remains convinced that IGN's training plan for the period 2015-2017 will allow it to improve its performance and better serve the population.

a4507.speaker: Noël Fonton, Minister responsible for Urban Planning, Housing and Sanitation of Benin
a4507.speech: Speaking of the document on the audit of the photovoltaic installations of Benin's permanent stations, recalled that they are a legacy of the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA) and that their management is entrusted to IGN: "These installations deserve our attention because they constitute the support network that ensures the reliability of data for sound and secure land management and, beyond that, for harmonious development of territorial planning," the minister stressed; he specifies that one of the important challenges of the continued operation of these permanent stations is energy, and that the audit will make it possible to rethink the photovoltaic installation arrangements in place today. The minister expressed the wish that, at the end of the proceedings, IGN's performance would improve and that it would have strategic management tools of the greatest importance.

a4507.speaker: Roch Abdon Bah, Director General of the Institut national géographique (IGN)
a4507.speech: Expressed to the authority the gratitude of all the staff for his leadership, then returned to the importance of the various documents to be validated for his organisation: "Without all this, it would just be flying blind. That is something IGN could not do," he concluded.

a4640.speaker: United States government
a4640.speech: Has announced a $450,000 grant to support emergency relief efforts in response to Tropical Cyclone Chido, which devastated parts of Mozambique in December last year.

a4640.speaker: Peter H. Vrooman, US ambassador
a4640.speech: Emphasized the importance of swift action to help those affected by Cyclone Chido. "The US government recognizes the immense challenges faced by the affected people and wants to reaffirm our solidarity. Our assistance will provide life-saving aid to those most impacted by the cyclone, helping to reduce human suffering and support recovery efforts."

a4647.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4647.speech: told top military leaders that it is not the role of American forces to police distant countries such as Somalia and Kenya, warning instead of a growing threat “from within.” “Only in recent decades did politicians somehow come to believe that our job is to police the far reaches of Kenya and Somalia, while America is under invasion from within” ; “We’re under invasion from within” ; “No different than a foreign enemy, but more difficult in many ways because they don’t wear uniforms. At least when they’re wearing a uniform you can take them out.”

a4647.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4647.speech: continues to advocate for the deployment of US military forces in major American cities. He has referred to violent elements in urban areas as “domestic terrorists” and has pledged to take strong action to curb rising crime and homicide rates across the country.

a4647.speaker: Somali authorities
a4647.speech: have consistently expressed concerns that a reduced US military presence could jeopardize security in the country and embolden Al-Shabaab.

a4647.speaker: Analysts (unnamed)
a4647.speech: warn that without sustained US support, Somalia’s fragile security gains could quickly unravel.

a4706.speaker: New study published in the scientific journal The Lancet
a4706.speech: Explains in detail how the gains made over the past two decades in reducing child and adult deaths could collapse following the formal closure of USAID; reports that between 2001 and 2021 USAID assistance helped reduce malaria and neglected diseases by more than 50 percent worldwide, that USAID funding reduced child deaths by 44 percent and deaths overall by an average of 15 percent, and that a total of 91 million deaths were averted, including 30 million deaths of children under five.

a4706.speaker: Researchers (authors of the Lancet study)
a4706.speech: "Our estimates show that, if the funding-cut measures announced and implemented in the first half of 2025 are not reversed, a large number of avoidable deaths could occur by 2030," the researchers said. ; "Our estimates are often higher because they take into account not only the direct effects of USAID health projects, as earlier studies did, but also the broader effects of USAID aid. These effects may have contributed greatly to this agency's success in reducing deaths," they explained.

a4706.speaker: Scientists (authors of the Lancet study)
a4706.speech: Said that between 2000 and 2023 deaths of children under five fell from 10.1 million to 4.8 million; however, they warn that halting USAID assistance could disrupt those gains and make it difficult to reach the Sustainable Development Goal of reducing child deaths to below 25 per 1,000 children by 2030.

a4706.speaker: Researchers (authors of the Lancet study)
a4706.speech: Warn that the effect of cutting off that aid is equivalent to a global pandemic or a major war, the difference being, they say, that this catastrophe can be prevented through a change of policy.

a4706.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a4706.speech: Announced the decision to close USAID through a 900-word speech titled "Make Foreign Aid Great Again", saying American citizens should not continue to pay taxes to support governments that do not work in faraway nations.

a4706.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4706.speech: Ordered the suspension of USAID's operations, under which much of the aid, largely in the health sector, has been halted.

a4831.speaker: Nasser Bourita, Morocco's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a4831.speech: stressed that military solutions would not resolve the Sudanese crisis; affirmed Morocco's solidarity with Sudan and its readiness to provide the necessary support to overcome the current crisis.

a4831.speaker: Nasser Bourita, Morocco's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a4831.speech: strongly pleaded for Morocco's commitment to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DRC: "The persistence of this instability compromises continental peace and security, jeopardising development efforts and regional cooperation, which obliges us all to act with determination and responsibility in order to initiate a dynamic of a peaceful, lasting and sustainable settlement of the conflict."

a4831.speaker: Nasser Bourita, Morocco's Minister of Foreign Affairs
a4831.speech: insisted on the need to remedy the suffering of civilians by facilitating humanitarian access to the affected populations: "Humanitarian aid must be delivered without obstacles, guaranteeing the protection of the populations," calling for coordinated efforts from the international community and regional actors.

a4831.speaker: Moroccan delegation to the AU Peace and Security Council
a4831.speech: successfully proposed a humanitarian truce during the coming month of Ramadan to allow unrestricted access for humanitarian aid to Sudan.

a4831.speaker: Morocco (government position)
a4831.speech: affirmed that dialogue and negotiation are important at this moment, expressing its firm opposition to any form of separatism, and called for an immediate cessation of hostilities, respect for the ceasefire and the resumption of negotiations in the DRC.

a5038.speaker: Muhammad Ali Pate, Nigeria's Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a5038.speech: Has long argued that no nation is secure if it imports the medicines on which its survival depends.

a5038.speaker: Bola Ahmed Tinubu, President of Nigeria (directive)
a5038.speech: Issued a directive, early this month and on advice from the Health Ministry, that no procurement, licence, or regulatory approval would proceed without proof of health insurance, making the NHIA certificate as essential as a tax ID.

a5083.speaker: Eskom (statement)
a5083.speech: The utility issued a statement noting that demand for the rest of the week would continue tight during evening peak hours which occur between 1730hrs and 1830hrs ; Eskom said the situation would ease going forward due to forecast milder temperatures.

a5083.speaker: Kitso Mokaila, Botswana Energy Minister
a5083.speech: Told a renewable energy conference that the 600MW Morupule B power station was fully up and running.

a5124.speaker: US Department of Defence (Pentagon) press statement
a5124.speech: Has said that Guantanamo Bay inmate Ridah Bin Saleh al-Yazidi has been repatriated to Tunisia; a press statement said he was found eligible for transfer from the detention facility after a "rigorous interagency review process" ; according to Monday's Pentagon statement, 26 detainees remain at Guantanamo Bay, of whom 14 are eligible for transfer.

a5124.speaker: The Pentagon (non-response)
a5124.speech: The Pentagon did not say if Yazidi had accepted any guilt.

a5124.speaker: The New York Times (unconfirmed report)
a5124.speech: According to an unconfirmed report, Yazidi was never charged and was approved for transfer more than a decade ago; the newspaper also said he had been at Guantanamo Bay since the facility was first set up in 2002.

a5124.speaker: Associated Press news agency
a5124.speech: Reported that earlier in December the Pentagon announced that the US had repatriated three other detainees.

a5164.speaker: Burundi (government)
a5164.speech: Was the first African country to congratulate Donald Trump on his election.

a5164.speaker: Democratic Republic of Congo (government)
a5164.speech: Added that it hopes the new president will not interfere in the internal politics of African countries.

a5164.speaker: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, President of Liberia
a5164.speech: Said she was worried, calling on President Trump not to call into question the various relations between the USA and Africa.

a5164.speaker: Burkina Faso (government)
a5164.speech: For its part stated that the new president-elect will have to work with the international community.

a5189.speaker: Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of Tanzania
a5189.speech: Speaking at the project site near the Mkuju River, highlighted the plant's strategic importance as it is expected to operate for 20 years, contributing significantly to the country's economy and energy resources ; revealed that the investment is projected to reach USD 1.2 billion, and that the economic benefits to Tanzania will include 750 permanent jobs, USD 373 million in royalties, USD 26 million in tree tax, USD 15.7 million in withholding tax, USD 1.01 billion in corporate tax, USD 20.8 million in license fees, and USD 40 million in government dividends from its equity stake annually.

a5189.speaker: Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of Tanzania
a5189.speech: Instructed that the project must strictly adhere to Tanzania's 2010 Mining Act (Cap. 123), particularly concerning local content and corporate social responsibility (CSR).

a5189.speaker: Nassoro Katuga, State Attorney (Tanzania)
a5189.speech: Requested another adjournment, citing the pending decision by the High Court expected on August 4, 2025 regarding a motion by the defense demanding the disclosure of anonymous witnesses ; “The High Court is expected to issue a ruling, and we must wait for that decision before proceeding. This court cannot override the High Court.”

a5189.speaker: Tundu Lissu, CHADEMA Chairman
a5189.speech: Strongly objected to the delay, arguing the court had been in favour of state counsels on unnecessarily prolonging the case ; argued that since investigations are complete, the case should be transferred to the High Court for hearing, or charges must be dropped ; further alleged that the repeated adjournments point to a coordinated effort to politically suppress him ahead of the general election.

a5189.speaker: Franco Kiswaga, Resident Magistrate, Kisutu Resident Magistrate's Court
a5189.speech: Has once again adjourned Case No. 8607/2025 involving the Republic versus CHADEMA Chairman Tundu Lissu, pushing the next hearing to August 13, 2025, when the court is expected to deliver a ruling on submissions made by both sides.

a5189.speaker: Residents of Nyatwali ward, Bunda District
a5189.speech: Have told The Chanzo that the relocation exercise has been marred by numerous irregularities, including brutality and severe human rights violations; that on July 26, 2025, two vehicles carrying 14 armed officers from the Tanzania National Parks Authority (TANAPA) arrived in two villages, Tamau and Serengeti, and that the officers allegedly beat residents, burned their homes, destroyed cattle enclosures, and forcibly removed livestock, abandoning them in unknown locations.

a5189.speaker: Mansoor Yussuf Himid and Ismail Jussa, members of the Maridhiano Committee (opinion piece)
a5189.speech: Wrote that fifteen years ago the people of Zanzibar voted with hope and conviction in a historic referendum that changed the course of the islands' political history, with 66.4 per cent of voters saying “YES” to a power-sharing system designed to end decades of political turmoil ; that the referendum was a profound national choice, a moment when Zanzibaris chose dialogue over division, peace over polarisation, culminating a courageous initiative led by then-President of Zanzibar Dr Amani Abeid Karume and the late Maalim Seif Sharif Hamad ; that as part of the team they witnessed firsthand the power of listening, compromise, and political courage, and that the fruit of that effort was the 10th Constitutional Amendment enshrining the Government of National Unity in Zanzibar's Constitution.

a5189.speaker: Summit of African liberation movements (press release)
a5189.speech: Concluded with calls to restrict arms exports to conflict zones and warnings against foreign interference on the continent, centred on concerns that Africa is being drawn into global conflicts, particularly through arms production and alleged foreign meddling in regional affairs.

a5189.speaker: Fikile Mbalula, ANC Secretary-General
a5189.speech: Said South Africa would block weapons shipments to war zones, including Ukraine ; “We have taken a decision—in line with South Africa's constitution and foreign policy—not to allow local arms manufacturers, whether state or private, to supply weapons to the conflict in Ukraine” ; described the move as a “pro-peace” stance rather than an anti-Western position.

a5235.speaker: Mondli Gungubele, Minister in the Presidency
a5235.speech: made the announcement on Thursday morning that Cabinet has approved the appointment of KwaZulu-Natal Cogta MEC Siphosihle Hlomuka as the national Cogta department's deputy director-general of local government support and interventions management, confirming this when he briefed the media on the outcome of a Cabinet meeting on Wednesday ; said Cabinet also approved a host of other appointments, subject to the verification of qualifications and the relevant clearance.

a5235.speaker: Cabinet (South Africa)
a5235.speech: commended the swift arrests made in connection with the murder of Hillary Gardee, the daughter of former EFF secretary-general Godrich Gardee ; also condemned the killing of six people in Khayelitsha, Cape Town.

a5235.speaker: Mondli Gungubele, Minister in the Presidency
a5235.speech: added that senseless murders were a reminder that more must be done to end gender-based violence and femicide (GBVF); he said Cabinet urged all people in the country to work with the government in the fight against crime and GBVF because a united front was the only way the country could put an end to such heinous crimes: "Together, we can ensure that our communities and streets are safer for all people, including the elderly, women and children."

a5235.speaker: Whistleblower (anonymous)
a5235.speech: raised allegations of corruption, collusion and interference with supply chain management processes concerning acting HDA CEO Daphney Ngoashen with HDA board chairperson Tshilidzi Ratshitanga and Human Settlements Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi in January.

a5235.speaker: Cabinet (South Africa)
a5235.speech: expressed condolences to those who lost loved ones in the floods, particularly those in KwaZulu-Natal.

a5235.speaker: Mondli Gungubele, Minister in the Presidency
a5235.speech: said the declaration of a national state of disaster and socio-economic relief interventions President Cyril Ramaphosa recently announced sought to ensure an effective and coordinated response across all spheres of government through the National Disaster Management Centre; he added that the R1 billion that the government made available was already in use to support relief and recovery efforts, restore basic services and provide humanitarian assistance in the form of food, water, shelter, sanitation and clothing ; "The process to rebuild affected areas has already started as the people of our country unite in their determination to assist those who have lost their homes and possessions."

a5235.speaker: Mondli Gungubele, Minister in the Presidency
a5235.speech: urged all citizens to take precautionary measures to protect themselves against Covid-19, especially during winter: "The virus is still a constant threat, and vaccination remains the most effective weapon to protect ourselves. The Cabinet is pleased that more people continue to choose vaccination as their first line of defence against Covid-19 after recent statistics showed that we had reached the milestone of over 50 percent of adult vaccinations in five provinces."

a5235.speaker: South African Government (@GovernmentZA), social media post
a5235.speech: "Join Minister Mondli Gungubele as he briefs media on outcomes of the cabinet meeting held on the 11th of May 2022.... #PostCab" (May 12, 2022).

a5245.speaker: United Nations
a5245.speech: says Somalia is among the most vulnerable to climate change, and that in the last five years it has experienced both the worst drought in 40 years and once-in-a-century flooding ; says its humanitarian needs for the year -- estimated at $1.4 billion -- are only 12 percent funded so far.

a5245.speaker: Mohamed Abdukadir Teesto, 43, Mogadishu resident whose home was flooded
a5245.speech: "We have cleaned our house using our bare hands," Teesto, 43, told AFP, saying neither international agencies nor the government had offered any assistance ; "Some families who had their houses destroyed are still displaced and cannot come back" ; "If it rains again, we will have the same situation."

a5245.speaker: Sara Cuevas Gallardo, spokesperson for the World Food Programme
a5245.speech: "This can get very, very bad, very quickly" ; "We don't know if we have the capacity" ; said Somalia could see a return to the situation in 2020-2023 when it was on the brink of famine, the difference being that now "we don't have the funds to actually act when we have to."

a5245.speaker: Sara Cuevas Gallardo, spokesperson for the World Food Programme
a5245.speech: Said that globally the main driver of hunger is conflict: "If it's mixed with the uncertainty of climate shocks in Somalia, then it just equals more food needs, more hunger, more people on the move, and us being unable to respond to that uncertainty as well."

a5245.speaker: CARE International
a5245.speech: said this month that Somalia had 1.8 million severely malnourished children under five, with 479,000 at risk of dying without urgent help.

a5245.speaker: International Crisis Group (ICG)
a5245.speech: has repeatedly warned about the link between climate change and conflict.

a5245.speaker: Save the Children (British charity)
a5245.speech: said last week that funding shortfalls would force it to shut more than a quarter of the health and nutrition facilities it runs in Somalia in the coming weeks, including every single one in the central city of Baidoa ; said that the current period always sees an uptick in malnourishment but this year it expects an 11-percent increase in malnutrition, leaving remaining facilities "stretched to breaking point."

a5245.speaker: Fatima, 25-year-old displaced mother (quoted by Save the Children)
a5245.speech: "If we were not able to get medicines and nutrition support here, we would have no other option but to see our children dying in front of us."

a5245.speaker: Mustafa Mohammed, doctor at a clinic in Baidoa
a5245.speech: said they have already seen a surge in patients and that closure would be grave: "There is nowhere else for these children to go."

a5527.speaker: Maryan Isman Ali, single disabled mother of five displaced in Aailow camp, Merka
a5527.speech: “Sometimes we get food to cook, sometimes we don’t. It’s a huge worry. I wake up in the morning and have nothing to cook. If you are a mother, you can feel the pain of me as a mother whose children are crying because of hunger and I have nothing to cook for them,” she told Radio Ergo.

a5527.speaker: Maryan Isman Ali, displaced mother in Aailow camp
a5527.speech: “Sometimes my young son, who is 10, fetches it for me. Sometimes my relatives do. We have a water problem. We also don’t have electricity and food — those are our specific needs. We don’t have a place to sleep; rain falls on us. We need everything. We need a lot of help.”

a5527.speaker: Maryan Isman Ali, displaced mother in Aailow camp
a5527.speech: “I don’t know what’s wrong with me. At night, I get a fever, my ribs hurt, and my condition is not good. Honestly, I need care, but I can’t afford medicine. When you go to the hospital, you have to pay to see the doctor, and medicines require money. We need everything,” she said.

a5527.speaker: Maryan Isman Ali, displaced mother in Aailow camp
a5527.speech: “I wish my children could be students and attend school but I can’t afford to send them. I can’t even manage Koranic classes. I can’t even afford the teacher’s salary for the school. I don’t even have food to eat so where would I get money for school? What I request is for my children to be sent to school so they can help me tomorrow.”

a5527.speaker: Maido Abdinur Hasan, displaced mother of six in the IDP camp
a5527.speech: Says she doesn’t know why the cash stopped, but it means she can’t feed her children: “I don’t have anything to give my children – I can’t even cook once a day. The children always cry for me, and I have nothing for them. I am really struggling to get them food. We are eating less than half what we used to eat. The children and I are in hardship together. When the children cry too much, the neighbours bring them a bowl of food, that’s how they survive,” she said.

a5527.speaker: Maido Abdinur Hasan, displaced mother of six
a5527.speech: “The shelter I live in is a makeshift hut made from trees we cut and gathered. It’s old, rotten, and we collected it from the neighbourhood. We use it to pray, but it doesn’t protect us from the rain, only the sun. If rain comes, we are in the worst situation.”

a5527.speaker: Abdi Osman Hasan, data collection worker with Marginalized Communities Advocacy Network (MCAN)
a5527.speech: Said that they had conveyed the needs of these families to ACTED, the international NGO that had been providing the funding for the monthly cash assistance; mentioned that they had registered many urgent cases in the camp, including children suffering from malnutrition after the aid stopped ; “We are pursuing it and following up with the organisation. We hope that something will reach these displaced people living in the camps soon.”

a5662.speaker: Sam Matekane, Prime Minister of Lesotho
a5662.speech: Has called on wool and mohair farmers to ramp up production as part of efforts to strengthen Lesotho's struggling economy; emphasized the government's unwavering support for the growth of the wool and mohair industry; underscored the significance of bringing banking services closer to rural communities, especially those active in wool and mohair farming: “This bank is here to serve you and offers products tailored to your needs” ; urged LPB to collaborate closely with local farmers to help their businesses thrive; reaffirmed the government's pledge not to interfere in wool and mohair affairs, instead promising to create an even playing field for all and provide necessary support: “We will support your businesses so you can reach your goals.”

a5662.speaker: Sam Matekane, Prime Minister of Lesotho
a5662.speech: Acknowledging the tough economic climate, partly caused by global trade disruptions, said the government was seeking new markets and opportunities to protect jobs and increase self-sufficiency; stressed the importance of improving livestock production, conserving pastures, upgrading school water and sanitation facilities, enhancing resource centres, and expanding electricity access through projects like Mission 300, supported by the World Bank; reiterated his administration's commitment to investing in agriculture, infrastructure, education, and social welfare; recognized the urgent need to repair deteriorating roads in Mokhotlong, describing roads as vital for trade and service delivery: “We know the era of relying on foreign aid is ending. It's time for us to join hands and build our economy together.”

a5697.speaker: J. Cyrus Saygbe, USAID Liberia’s Private Sector Specialist, Economic Growth
a5697.speech: In a statement, highlighted the funding's goal to translate innovative concepts into practical solutions, generate employment, enhance food security, and stimulate economic development in Liberia; emphasized the significance of the agribusiness pitching competition in showcasing the credibility and potential of Liberia’s agribusiness sector; praised the participants for serving as inspiration to others ; “I encourage you to step forward with confidence and bring the brilliance of Liberia’s entrepreneurship regardless of all, your dedication and hard work already position you as leaders in the field. You are an inspiration to others and a testament to the potential that exists within Liberia's agriculture sector.”

a5697.speaker: Wainright Acquoi, CEO of TRIBE
a5697.speech: expressed appreciation for the participants' commitment to the challenging competition; emphasized that the Monrovia Startup Consortium (MSC) is honored to collaborate with these individuals to generate employment, alleviate poverty, and address vital issues throughout Liberia; extended his gratitude to USAID and the Africa Trade and Investment (ATI) Activity for their essential support ; “This pitch competition is more than a showcase of ideas; it's a testament to the resilience and innovation of Liberia’s entrepreneurs. These grants are not just funding—they're investments in solutions that tackle pressing challenges, create jobs, and ignite sustainable growth.”

a5697.speaker: Grant recipients / beneficiaries
a5697.speech: The recipients expressed that the grant would provide them with increased economic freedom and sustainability for their businesses; beneficiaries expressed gratitude for the support, emphasizing the impact the grants will have on expanding their businesses and addressing market demands.

a5697.speaker: James O. Gaygay, Finance Manager of Patience Cocoa Inc.
a5697.speech: expressed gratitude for the US$25,000 grant, stating that the funds would be instrumental in acquiring equipment to address production demands; highlighted past challenges in fulfilling orders from larger companies due to financial constraints ; “Sometimes, other companies reach out to us, but we don’t have what it takes to meet their demands. With this $25,000, we are very sure we will fulfill those demands and more.”

a5697.speaker: Akouavi Tehoungue, CEO of Jimmy Snacks Kitchen Inc.
a5697.speech: highlighted the financial difficulties her business has encountered in recent months; expressed her plans to utilize the grant to enhance their business operations and expand their market reach, aiming to restock shelves in supermarkets and extend their presence beyond Montserrado to cover all fifteen counties; acknowledged TRIBE and its partners for providing valuable training in financial management and sourcing.

a5765.speaker: Malawi Congress Party (MCP) manifesto, launched by President Lazarus Chakwera
a5765.speech: Pledges to transform lives through the Tsogolo Account, an expanded Constituency Development Fund (CDF) and large-scale social interventions, including K500 000 for every newborn, three million jobs, more funds for every constituency and expanded bursaries and social protection schemes for the poor ; hints at taxing alcohol and tobacco and broadening the tax net

a5765.speaker: Mavuto Bamusi, policy and governance activist
a5765.speech: “This is a continuation of a bad habit of promising without first accounting for previous failures” (when asked about Chakwera’s new manifesto)

a5765.speaker: Mavuto Bamusi, policy and governance activist
a5765.speech: Warns of the Tsogolo Account: “This is a consumption-based pledge that cannibalises development expenditure. At a time when dialysis machines are absent from all district hospitals and malnutrition remains the leading killer of under-fives, giving out cash to infants is not only tone-deaf; it is dangerous.”

a5765.speaker: George Chaima, political analyst
a5765.speech: “As the MCP government has failed to demonstrate that one million jobs were created, it is just a fallacy to come again and promise over three million jobs.”

a5765.speaker: George Chaima, political analyst
a5765.speech: Argues the Tsogolo Account “lacks the economic factor for wealth creation”: “If K500 000 is deposited today, by the time the child turns 18, it will be worth maybe $10 or $15 (about K17 000 and K25 000 at current exchange rate). That’s not empowerment. It is political theatre” ; warns the promise could backfire socially: “It may encourage high and active sexual activity just to produce more babies. How will the national and global concern over population control be addressed?”

a5765.speaker: George Chaima, political analyst
a5765.speech: Questions the government’s basic priorities: “Where will they get that kind of money when they are struggling to put medicine in hospitals, when there are no desks in schools, no bridges in rural areas?” ; “In my view, the MCP manifesto cannot be implemented within five years” ; favours policy reforms that empower Malawians to build the nation with their own hands instead of entrenching a culture of handouts: “Malawi is not a refugee camp. We are a sovereign State and we need to eat food produced by ourselves, not live off handouts. You can’t build a nation based on food and cash distribution. This kind of politics brings more oppression because even the distribution process itself lacks transparency.”

a5765.speaker: Dalitso Kubalasa, economic governance and policy analyst
a5765.speech: “There’s a significant gap between what’s been promised in the past and what is being offered now. Making grand promises without the necessary systems in place could stretch an already fragile public budget too thin.”

a5765.speaker: Dalitso Kubalasa, economic governance and policy analyst
a5765.speech: Calls the manifesto’s optimism “a fiscal mirage”: “The country is grappling with an aid freeze, over K17 trillion in public debt and stagnant domestic revenue. We cannot afford political fantasy disguised as policy” ; warns: “CDF, now at K200 million per constituency, is fast becoming a vehicle for political appeasement, not development. If left unchecked, it could entrench corruption while starving essential programmes of investment” ; reckons the country’s problem is not dreaming big but failing to act honestly: “Malawi has the vision. What it lacks is the ability to execute, the honesty to prioritise and the courage to reject what is unsustainable. Let’s build a coalition that includes youth leaders, civil society, faith groups and the private sector—not as bystanders but as drivers of change.”

a5765.speaker: Dr Nandini Patel, political scientist
a5765.speech: Agrees the three million jobs promise feels far-fetched, but remains optimistic: “Many school blocks have indeed been constructed under this administration. That infrastructure can absorb more teachers and give thousands of children decent classrooms. We must be careful not to dismiss everything as failure” ; calls the Tsogolo Account and expanded bursaries “sheer campaign tools”, not transformative investments

a5775.speaker: Faizal Sidat, President of the Mozambican Football Federation (FMF)
a5775.speech: Does not reveal whether or not he will renew with Chiquinho Conde as national football team coach; accuses the coach of disrespect towards him and other members of the FMF board, and stresses that the renewal with Chiquinho is still subject to internal debate.

a5775.speaker: Dan Moyane, South African journalist
a5775.speech: Believes that South Africa will continue to be a good partner of Mozambique and of all the countries in the region.

a5775.speaker: European Commissioner for International Cooperation
a5775.speech: Gave the information this Wednesday, at the end of a two-day visit to Mozambique, that the European Union is studying the possibility of sending observers for the general elections of 9 October and of increasing financial support for the Rwandan troops in Cabo Delgado.

a5775.speaker: United States Agency for International Development (USAID)
a5775.speech: Celebrated this Tuesday forty years of partnership with Mozambique, recalling landmark moments and challenges for the times ahead.

a5775.speaker: Minister of Health of Mozambique (representing the Government)
a5775.speech: Said that the partnership [with USAID] made it possible to develop various areas of the country, with emphasis on health and education.

a5775.speaker: Bank of Mozambique (new foreign exchange law)
a5775.speech: The idea in the new exchange law is to eliminate barriers to foreign direct investment and to stimulate the foreign exchange market: foreign citizens may now invest in Mozambique without prior authorisation from the Central Bank, but only if the amounts involved are equal to or less than one million US dollars.

a5831.speaker: Retselisitsoe Matlanyane, Minister of Finance and Development Planning of Lesotho (budget speech)
a5831.speech: Did not disclose the specific budget allocation for the dumpsite's rehabilitation. However, she mentioned that the government was conducting studies on the Tsoeneng Landfill as an alternative: "The intention is to explore all available options for sustainable waste management, which could be implemented not only for Tsoeneng and Tsosane but across the country. Preparatory works to close the Tsosane dumpsite and operationalize Tsoeneng are planned and budgeted for the 2025/2026 financial year."

a5831.speaker: Portfolio Committees on Law and Public Safety, Natural Resources and Tourism, and Land Clusters
a5831.speech: Declared the Tsosane dump site illegal in November last year. They said it had been operating without an environmental impact assessment or clearance certificate, violating the Environmental Act of 2008.

a5831.speaker: Ntaote Moru, area chief of Letsatseng in Ha Tsosane
a5831.speech: Expressed frustration with the government's inaction. He lamented the growing infestation of nearby homes by rats and cockroaches from the dumpsite: "Why continue dumping waste at an already out-of-control dumpsite when they claim to have plans for rehabilitation?" ; "We were expecting the government to stop dumping waste here in preparation for the rehabilitation, but instead, it continues as if nothing is wrong. We endure the terrible smell from rotting meat and dead animals, while rats and cockroaches invade our homes daily." ; "Even with this budget speech, we are not convinced that this place will be rehabilitated. This is not the first time we've been told money will be set aside to rehabilitate the site and relocate the dumpsite to Tsoeneng. It's been years of empty promises."

a5831.speaker: Ntaote Moru, area chief of Letsatseng in Ha Tsosane
a5831.speech: Said that despite their efforts to stop the dumping, such as blocking roads and restricting access to the site, their attempts were thwarted when police and soldiers intervened. He recalled promises made by Cabinet minister, Limpho Tau, who had assured that rehabilitation would have already started by now, yet nothing had changed. He also said the community had even approached the courts for intervention, but their concerns remained unresolved.

a5831.speaker: Ntaote Moru, area chief of Letsatseng in Ha Tsosane
a5831.speech: Pointed out that surrounding communities had given up farming due to the damage caused by the rats from the dumpsite: "These are not just ordinary rats. They are massive, and they even eat other rats and food in the fields. The Maseru City Council promised to fumigate homes in the area, but only a few households received treatment, leaving the rest to suffer the infestation."

a5831.speaker: Masechabe Tlome, 77-year-old lifelong resident of Ha Tsosane
a5831.speech: Stated that the poor management of the dumpsite had drastically affected her quality of life: "There's nothing we can do. I live here, and I have nowhere else to go. The smell and smoke often seep through the house, even when we've closed the doors and windows. Some people have fallen ill due to the constant exposure to these fumes. Sometimes, mischievous boys set the waste on fire, or it explodes on its own. Given the location of my house, I'm always afraid that it might catch fire."

a5831.speaker: Sehloho Letsielo, resident of Ha Tsosane
a5831.speech: Urged the government to provide regular free medical check-ups and fumigate their homes, which were overrun with rats and cockroaches from the dumpsite. He said elderly people and children were particularly vulnerable to respiratory diseases caused by the fumes but could not afford medical care: "We request that the government at least provide a mobile clinic quarterly, so that the community, especially children and the elderly, can be tested for respiratory-related diseases caused by the fumes and smell from the dumpsite." ; "We also ask that while they prepare for the rehabilitation of the dumpsite, they better manage the site and, if possible, stop adding waste to the already overwhelmed dumpsite. It's not fair that we're being subjected to health risks from waste collected from across the district, especially when we manage our own waste responsibly. It would be more understandable if the waste was our own and we were dealing with the consequences of our own negligence."

a5831.speaker: 'Makatleho Mosala, Maseru City Council (MCC) spokesperson
a5831.speech: Told the Lesotho Times there were challenges but said the evacuation of the dump to Tsoeneng was a multi-step process: "There are procedures that need to be followed, and we are carrying it out in phases. Currently, we are conducting a visibility study to guide the conditions under which the Tsoeneng site will be developed." ; She claimed they had already addressed some of the community's concerns, such as the bad smell, rats, and cockroaches: "We have changed our dumping methods to reduce the odour and have fumigated households to address the rat and cockroach issues. People were asked to register their names so their homes could be treated."

a5961.speaker: Nuhu Ribadu’s lawyer (lawyer to Nigeria’s National Security Adviser)
a5961.speech: Demanded a public apology and retraction of Haj. Naja’atu Mohammed’s TikTok video.

a5961.speaker: Haj. Naja’atu Mohammed, northern political stalwart
a5961.speech: Recalled in a TikTok video that the NSA had called Tulumbu the “most corrupt politician” when he was EFCC Chairman; clarified that she would not retract her statement against Ribadu and made another video saying that what she said was what the NSA had said years ago.

a5961.speaker: Kano State Deputy Governor
a5961.speech: Quickly apologised when the NSA threatened a court case following his allegation about the NSA’s involvement in the Kano Emirate crisis.

a5961.speaker: Nuhu Ribadu, Nigeria’s National Security Adviser
a5961.speech: Publicly told the Canadian High Commission in Nigeria “to go to hell” after its embassy denied visas to the Chief of Defence Staff, Christopher Musa, and some high military command officers.

a5961.speaker: A report / the Canadian embassy in Nigeria
a5961.speech: Shows that the Canadian embassy refused to give the military officers visas because protocols were not followed; the embassy expected the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to issue a “note verbale” as a supporting document for their application.

a5961.speaker: Tigran Gambaryan, Binance’s head of financial crime (posts on X)
a5961.speech: Made a huge allegation about the NSA in a series of tweets, claiming that Mr Ribadu hired a US law firm to negotiate his release from Nigerian detention, but the move failed due to the NSA’s “incompetence and greed”: “Ribadu emphasised that he wanted billions in payouts to fund his future political ambition. However, when the corruption scandal came to light, he was trapped—because any settlement would now be perceived as a bribe. I guess he really wanted his boss’s job.”

a5961.speaker: Scott Perry, US Congressman
a5961.speech: Went public with a strong claim that the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was funding terrorist organisations, including Boko Haram, ISIS, and Al-Qaeda.

a5961.speaker: Nuhu Ribadu and his lawyers (non-response)
a5961.speech: Have found a way to avoid shame by remaining silent over Naja’atu Mohammed’s refusal to retract, and have yet to respond to Gambaryan’s allegation; the NSA has also kept mum and made no statement on the USAID/Boko Haram allegations.

a6026.speaker: Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA)
a6026.speech: Said Wednesday it had lost $40 million in grants following aid cuts by US President Donald Trump.

a6026.speaker: Alice Ruhweza, AGRA president
a6026.speech: Told AFP that cuts to US foreign aid would significantly hit the organisation, which has been operating since 2011. "Reduced resources from USAID means that all that groundwork… will be affected," she said, adding that other major funders from European countries were also cutting back ; "We're getting a lot of these messages all the time: 'Sorry, we are reducing (funding).'"

a6026.speaker: Alice Ruhweza, AGRA president
a6026.speech: Said the aid cut by the US was a "wake-up call" for African countries to invest in agriculture, describing it as its "engine of economic growth" ; "If we invest our resources well, we probably don't need aid."

a6026.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)
a6026.speech: Said it was suspending aid for 650,000 malnourished women and children in Ethiopia because of a lack of funding ; warned they were among 3.6 million people in Ethiopia who would no longer have access to food aid in the coming weeks without urgent new funding.

a6026.speaker: Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)
a6026.speech: Said development assistance had already been dropping worldwide before the USAID cuts ; aid fell by 7.1 percent between 2023 and 2024, it said — the first decline in six years, as multiple countries slashed their budgets.

a6052.speaker: Yacouba Soukeyradjou, Secretary General of the Governorate of Tahoua
a6052.speech: In his introductory remarks, on behalf of the region's Governor, Colonel-Major Souleymane Amadou Moussa, who was unable to attend, reported that the Governor is very satisfied with the work done by the various organising commissions of the 2025 national tree festival; said that for this reason all the commissions are being maintained for this ceremony, with some small readjustments including the creation of a communication commission and a change in the presidency of the regional committee; then set out the objective of the meeting, which is to agree on the name the market will bear, which had been proposed beforehand by the Chief of the Canton of Tahoua; and gave as second information the arrival of the Minister of Trade and Industry, scheduled for Sunday 17 August, to take part in the inauguration and naming ceremony of the modern market of Tahoua.

a6052.speaker: Sahabi Moussa, Administrative Delegate (AD) of the City of Tahoua
a6052.speech: Announced the contribution of the City of Tahoua to the total success of the ceremony.

a6052.speaker: Regional Director of Trade
a6052.speech: Thanked all those who responded to the invitation as well as the regional authorities, while informing them of the agenda of the Minister of Trade and Industry for this trip to Tahoua: in addition to taking part in the inauguration and naming ceremony of the modern market of Tahoua, Minister Abdoulaye Seydou is to visit certain industrial units in the Tahoua region, notably in the city of Tahoua, but also the reinforcing-steel plants and the Mango cement works of Badaguichiri, the MCC cement works of Malbaza and the onion depot of Tsernaoua (Konni).

a6237.speaker: UN agencies and aid groups
a6237.speech: Said on Tuesday that food insecurity and acute malnutrition in Somalia has not reached "IPC Phase 5 Famine" levels between October and December 2022, although the situation there is still a crisis.

a6237.speaker: Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) report
a6237.speech: Said that following the commendable response efforts of humanitarian actors and local communities, the food insecurity and acute malnutrition situation has not reached famine levels; said 214 000 people in Somalia were classified as being in IPC Phase 5 Catastrophe in October-December, expected to rise to 322 000 in January-March and 727 000 in April-June amid an anticipated reduction in funding for humanitarian assistance; said Phase 5 Famine was projected in April-June among agropastoral populations in Baidoa and Burhakaba districts and displaced populations in Baidoa town of Bay region and in Mogadishu, adding that these population groups are already experiencing very high levels of acute malnutrition and mortality.

a6237.speaker: Humanitarian organisations
a6237.speech: Have warned for months that parts of Somalia's Bay region were on the verge of famine because of the impact of a two-year drought, compounded by rising global grain prices and a long-running Islamist insurgency.

a6237.speaker: Some aid workers
a6237.speech: Have warned that this time could be even worse than in 2011.

a6309.speaker: Alberto Wilde, Country Director of Global Communities
a6309.speech: Said the water systems represent more than just infrastructure as they signify progress and a better quality of life for the residents; said with the provision of accessible water, parents and school children will now spend less time in search of water and live a dignified life. "These water systems represent more than just infrastructure; they signify hope, progress, and a better quality of life for the residents of Nawuhugu and Nanton Kurugu. With clean and safe drinking water now readily available, families can enjoy improved health outcomes, children can attend school regularly without the burden of water collection, and communities can thrive and prosper" ; "As we celebrate this milestone today, let us also reaffirm our commitment to continue working together to address the challenges of water accessibility and sanitation in Ghana. Together, we can build a future where every individual has access to this basic human right."

a6309.speaker: Some of the residents of Nawulugu and Nanton-Kurugu
a6309.speech: Indicated that the water problem in the community was a daily hurdle and commended USAID and partners for the gesture.

a6309.speaker: Sulemana Margaret, a resident of Nawulugu
a6309.speech: "Sometimes we do go for a mile or two to get water, if you go in the morning, you may come in the evening or the next morning, sometime we sleep there just to get water. And sometimes the water will not be potable so we normally put alum, and we were getting Guinea worm and our children if they drink their teeth become brown."

a6309.speaker: Amidu Issahaku Chinnia, Deputy Minister of Sanitation and Water Resources
a6309.speech: Said the government is committed to providing potable water to the citizenry by 2030 and commended private partners for complementing the effort of the government in that regard.

a6309.speaker: Kimberly Rosen, USAID Mission Director
a6309.speech: Indicated that the initiative marks a significant expansion of access to clean water and sanitation facilities, furthering the organization's commitment to improving the quality of life in underserved regions. She said, "over the next few years, USAID will provide safe water access to Ghana's half million people, the two water systems we are honouring today is part of those efforts."

a6441.speaker: Dr. Jok Madut Jok, Professor of Anthropology at Syracuse University
a6441.speech: Said should Washington proceed with the plan, it would be bad news for South Sudanese and undermine America's ability to monitor and address negative developments in the country ; expressed concern over reports that the Trump administration is considering the move, saying such a move reflects a broader policy shift by the inward-looking Trump administration and the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in its cost-cutting approach to global engagement ; "I should also add that should this policy come to pass, and the embassies close down in Juba, such an eventuality would be bad for South Sudan in many respects." ; "It would mean that the US can no longer bear witness to the many negative developments and challenges in the country, such as famine, disease, violence, and human rights abuses, and other undemocratic practices that the South Sudan government sometimes pursues." ; "It would mean that this is now a true severing of engagement between the two peoples, and the cultural exchanges would simply diminish. The research exchanges would also be lost." ; expressed relief at the vagueness of the document because the White House and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are yet to formally approve the decision.

a6441.speaker: Dr. Jok Madut Jok, Professor of Anthropology at Syracuse University
a6441.speech: Further questioned the rationale behind the proposed withdrawal of American diplomatic presence from regions grappling with instability and conflict, suggesting that this move may not be based on comprehensive policy analysis, but rather on the administration's ideological drive to reduce international commitments and government spending, and that the Trump administration may have not viewed South Sudan as a priority due to limited trade relations and minimal commercial interests: "Perhaps the Trump administration does not really care about these things, as its interests have always been commercial, and since South Sudan does not have much trade with the US, perhaps Washington does not see any utility in continued engagement with Juba." ; "So, this policy might, on the face of it, look detrimental to the relationships, but deep down, Washington is probably convinced that South Sudan does not really present any kind of value that is worth investing in."

a6441.speaker: Internal State Department document (first reported by CNN)
a6441.speech: Indicated that the U.S. is weighing at closing nearly 30 overseas embassies and consulates, as the Trump administration eyes significant changes to its diplomatic presence abroad ; also recommends reducing the footprint at the US diplomatic missions in Somalia and Iraq where the US is engaged in counterterrorism efforts, and resizing other diplomatic outposts ; the draft proposal recommends shutting down 10 embassies and 17 consulates, including those in the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Lesotho, and South Sudan, with the responsibilities of the closed embassies reassigned to U.S. missions in neighbouring countries.

a6441.speaker: Separate memo cited by the Associated Press
a6441.speech: According to the memo, the Trump administration is also eliminating more than 90% of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)'s foreign aid contracts and $60 billion in overall U.S. assistance around the world.

a6441.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a6441.speech: On January 20, ordered a 90-day program-by-program review of which foreign assistance programs deserved to continue and which must be eliminated.

a6441.speaker: Office of Management and Budget (OMB)
a6441.speech: Is further proposing to cut funding for United Nations peacekeeping missions, citing recent failures in operations across Africa and the Middle East, including in Mali, Lebanon, and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

a6528.speaker: Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi, Egyptian President
a6528.speech: Reaffirmed his rejection of any regional escalation and called for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza, the delivery of humanitarian aid, and the securing of the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

a6528.speaker: Abbas Araghchi, Iranian Foreign Minister
a6528.speech: At a joint press conference with his Egyptian counterpart Badr Abdelatty, underlined Iran's commitment to diplomacy, while defending the continuation of uranium enrichment for peaceful purposes ; welcomed Egypt's mediation efforts and raised the possibility of a restoration of full diplomatic relations, “when the conditions are met”.

a6528.speaker: Egypt (government position)
a6528.speech: Reiterated its support for a Middle East free of nuclear weapons and its attachment to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

a6598.speaker: Dephue Zuo, Deputy Finance Minister for Economic Management of Liberia
a6598.speech: Named the diplomatic community in Monrovia, the UN, civil society, and the private sector, among others, as stakeholders expected to attend the gathering.

a6598.speaker: Dephue Zuo, Deputy Finance Minister for Economic Management of Liberia
a6598.speech: Told the MICAT Press Briefing on Tuesday, April 15, 2025, that the goal of the retreat is to brainstorm on strategic ways in which the government can realign funding to address gaps that were created by the Trump Administration's aid cut ; disclosed that the government anticipates having a technical session after the retreat with all parties to the preparation of the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID) ; “President Joseph Boakai is keen on ensuring that the implementation of the AAID is more inclusive, creative, innovative, and effective.”

a6732.speaker: Government of Mozambique
a6732.speech: The Mozambican government has pledged to complete, this year, the construction of houses for families removed from the vicinity of the Hulene dump, where 16 people died when the dump collapsed in February 2018.

a6732.speaker: Filimão Suaze, Mozambican cabinet spokesperson
a6732.speech: “We believe the houses will be completed in 2020,” cabinet spokesperson Filimão Suaze said after the Council of Ministers meeting in Maputo on Tuesday.

a6732.speaker: Filimão Suaze, Mozambican cabinet spokesperson
a6732.speech: “The disbursement aims to ensure the payment of rent while houses in the resettlement area are completed,” Filimão Suaze announced, without however detailing exact figures.

a6732.speaker: Government of Mozambique (2018 announcement)
a6732.speech: The same year (2018), the Mozambican government announced that the dump would be closed, at the cost of US$110 million (€98 million at current exchange rates).

a6918.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a6918.speech: Demands that all individuals involved in financial crimes in the Public Administration be held accountable, and wants greater strategic coordination and information sharing between the Administrative Court and the bodies of justice administration and investigation in order to eliminate barriers in the fight against fraud and corruption.

a6918.speaker: Emilia Moiane, director of the information office (Gabinete de Informacao)
a6918.speech: Said, presiding over the swearing-in of Orlando Gambeta as new director general of AIM this Wednesday in Maputo, that AIM, the Mozambican news agency, must position itself in the mission of promoting the country's achievements, the consolidation of national unity, the national interests, and the promotion of democracy and social justice.

a6918.speaker: Banana producers in Gorongosa
a6918.speech: Are calling for harmonisation of the selling price of bananas, and want them to be sold by the kilogram and not by the bunch.

a7085.speaker: Jeanne Shaheen, U.S. Senator (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee
a7085.speech: Took to the Senate floor to mark the second anniversary of the civil war in Sudan, calling on the U.S. to resume foreign and humanitarian assistance to the region, help put an end to the conflict and set Sudan back on a path to a civilian-led democracy: “In the two years since, over 150,000 people have died and 12 million more have been displaced. And you can see this poster reflects the results of what's happening in Sudan. [In] just two years, 12 million more people have been displaced and are in camps… With acute famine levels at historic highs, 30 million people are in desperate need of humanitarian aid.” ; recounted that back in 2018 Sudanese citizens took to the streets to protest conditions, pushing Omar al-Bashir out of power, before the military overthrew the civilian-led government and, two years ago, the Sudanese Armed Forces led by General al-Burhan and the Rapid Support Forces led by General Hemedti plunged Sudan into war.

a7085.speaker: Jeanne Shaheen, U.S. Senator (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee
a7085.speech: “As so often happens during war, the impact has been especially devastating to women and girls. During raids by the armed factions, women and girls have been abducted and forced into sexual and domestic slavery. One UN report found gender-based violence skyrocketed by 288% last year.” ; said that if the UNICEF finding that 221 children have been raped, including a case involving a 1-year-old baby, is true, “we just can't ignore it as another horrific detail of a distant conflict. The world is watching and we must hold the people perpetrating these acts accountable for their crimes.”

a7085.speaker: Jeanne Shaheen, U.S. Senator (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee
a7085.speech: Said that in January 2025 the U.S. Treasury Department took a positive step by sanctioning the leader of the Rapid Support Forces and the leader of the Sudanese Armed Forces for their armies' lethal attacks on civilians, “But more needs to be done. Ceasefire after ceasefire has failed. Peace negotiations have stalled. And outside countries—the UAE, Turkey, Iran as well as Russia and China—continue to send weapons to the factions. Now why? Well because Russia doesn't want to give up its port access on the Red Sea, China does not want to abandon the nearly six billion dollars of investments it has made since 2005, and the UAE doesn't want to abandon Sudan's wartime gold trade.” ; said “The United States needs to stand up and say, ‘enough is enough’”, arguing that “what happens in Africa, what happens in Sudan, doesn't stay in Sudan. If you can't be outraged because of the moral horror of what's happening there, you should be outraged because the terrorism, the potential disease—that can cross the borders of Sudan, that can come to the United States.”

a7085.speaker: Jeanne Shaheen, U.S. Senator (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee
a7085.speech: “As Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, I am committed to working with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle here in Congress as well as with folks in the Trump Administration. Because we must hold these groups accountable for their war crimes. We must support them in ending the violence.” ; said both sides continue to bomb, raid and siege schools, markets and hospitals, the Sudanese Armed Forces are intentionally denying humanitarian aid and blocking medicine and other relief items, the Rapid Support Forces continue an ethnically charged campaign of violence in Darfur, and “sadly, so many of the foreign assistance programs that we had in place have been ended or are under review” ; “The U.S., the Trump Administration and Congress must create a clear policy to address this conflict. We must resume foreign assistance to the region and Sudan to limit further humanitarian suffering. And we must set aside our differences, bring an end to the violence and renew our commitment to setting Sudan back on the path to a civilian-led democracy.”

a7085.speaker: UN report
a7085.speech: Found that gender-based violence skyrocketed by 288% last year.

a7085.speaker: UNICEF
a7085.speech: Cited as reporting that 221 children have been raped — including a case involving a 1-year-old baby.

a7085.speaker: United States government (determination)
a7085.speech: Has determined that both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during fighting in Sudan, and that the Rapid Support Forces led a campaign of ethnic cleansing in Darfur.

a7085.speaker: Mining industry sources and research by SWISSAID
a7085.speech: Cited as the source that nearly all of Sudan's gold trade flows through the UAE.
